title: Closer application: the doubt syllogism and two senses of uncertainty
source_text: XXIII. Sed, ut jam pressius agamus, ista sunt ad argumentum propositum applicanda. Argumentum fuit ejusmodi. Quod ex se nobis est dubium & incertum firma fide a nobis apprehendi non potest, nisi authoritate aliqua superiori confirmetur. Sed Scriptura ex se nobis dubia & incerta est. Ergo necesse est eam authoritate aliqua superiori confirmari. Quae alia esse non potest quam Ecclesiae authoritas. Respondeo aliquid nobis dubium & incertum dici potest duplici respectu. Nempe fidei respectu: deinde respectu rationis humanae. Fidei incertum est quod a Deo revelatum & inspiratum non est. At rationi humanae incertum est quod demonstrari non potest argumentis necessariis & evidentibus. Itaque distinguenda minor, Scriptura ex se nobis dubia & incerta. Nam, si illud nobis dicatur, respectu rationis humanae concedi potest, si vero respectu fidei neganda est. Quamvis enim Scriptura rationi etiam humanae suaderi & commendari possit multis bonis & validis argumentis: Attamen quia ista argumenta logice & mathematice demonstrativa non sunt, eatenus patimur Scripturam dici humanae rationi incertam. Sed falsum est fidei non posse esse certum quod rationi incertum est, nec demonstrari potest. Imo quod demonstrari potest eatenus res fidei non est.
pass_a_gloss: But so that we may now deal more closely, these things are to be applied to the proposed argument. The argument was of this kind. What of itself is doubtful and uncertain to us cannot be apprehended by us with firm faith unless it is confirmed by some superior authority. But Scripture of itself is doubtful and uncertain to us. Therefore it is necessary that it be confirmed by some superior authority. Which can be nothing else than the authority of the Church. I answer that something can be said to be doubtful and uncertain to us in a twofold respect. Namely with respect to faith; then with respect to human reason. Uncertain to faith is what has not been revealed and inspired by God. But uncertain to human reason is what cannot be demonstrated by necessary and evident arguments. Therefore the minor is to be distinguished: Scripture of itself is doubtful and uncertain to us. For if that is said to us with respect to human reason, it can be conceded; but if with respect to faith, it is to be denied. For although Scripture can also be urged and recommended to human reason by many good and valid arguments: nevertheless because those arguments are not logically and mathematically demonstrative, to that extent we allow Scripture to be called uncertain to human reason. But it is false that what is uncertain to reason, and cannot be demonstrated, cannot be certain to faith. Indeed what can be demonstrated is to that extent not a matter of faith.
pass_b_english: But to deal more closely now, apply this to the argument on the table. It runs like this: what is doubtful and uncertain to us of itself cannot be firmly believed unless some higher authority confirms it; Scripture of itself is doubtful and uncertain to us; therefore some higher authority must confirm it — and that can only be the Church.
I answer that something can be called doubtful and uncertain to us in two respects: with respect to faith, and with respect to human reason.

Uncertain for faith is what God has not revealed and inspired. Uncertain for human reason is what cannot be shown by necessary and evident proofs. So distinguish the minor: Scripture of itself is doubtful and uncertain to us. Said of human reason, that can be granted; said of faith, it must be denied.

Scripture can of course be urged on human reason with many good, weighty arguments. Because those arguments are not logical or mathematical demonstrations, we allow that Scripture may be called uncertain to human reason. But it is false that what reason finds uncertain and indemonstrable cannot be certain for faith. What can be demonstrated is, to that extent, not a matter of faith at all.

choices.why: Closer application of the prior reply.

choices.english: with respect to / in the respect of
